r.x: Good-Bye Cigarettes, Hello Pipe

is a newsletter piece signed by Steve Fallon that appeared in The Pipe Collector, the publication of the North American Society of Pipe Collectors (NASPC), and was later reproduced on Pipedia with the society's permission. It is among the most frequently cited examples of a belief that has circulated in the community across generations: the notion that someone wanting to quit cigarettes might find the answer in the pipe. This entry treats the text not as an advice source but as a document belonging to the community writing of its time; it neither repeats nor endorses its recommendations.
The Document's Identity

The piece came not from a physician or a smoking-cessation program but from a collector's pen, addressed to fellow society members; its genre is the familiar experience-sharing piece found in newsletters. Because the Pipedia page is published with NASPC's permission, copyright in the text belongs to the society; here only the piece's identity and its central claim are noted. This kind of writing was common in collector newsletters in the last quarter of the 20th century. The shared assumption is that the pipe is a pursuit distinct from cigarettes — that one is a habit and the other a pleasure — and it is from this distinction that presenting a product switch as a solution arises.
The Underlying Nicotine Assumption

The technical basis of the claim is that the two smoking methods deliver nicotine at different speeds. Nicotine in smoke drawn into the lungs crosses into arterial blood through the lung's large absorption surface and reaches the brain in roughly ten to twenty seconds; this rapid peak is considered central to reinforcing dependence. Pipe smoke has traditionally not been drawn into the lungs but tasted in the mouth; absorption through the oral mucosa is both slower and produces a lower peak level. Smoke acidity plays a role in this difference as well: nicotine in alkaline smoke crosses the oral mucosa more easily, while in acidic smoke absorption depends largely on the respiratory route. Nicotine content also varies among pipe tobacco blends; Burley- and Virginia-forward blends generally deliver more, while Latakia- and oriental-forward blends deliver less.
Comparison with Public-Health Data

The text's most problematic aspect today is its treatment of inhaling part of the smoke during the transition as unremarkable. Public-health literature warns precisely on this point: those who switch from cigarettes to cigars or pipes tend to carry over their old inhaling habit, and this behavior largely cancels out the reduction in risk expected from a product switch. In a large American cohort, cigar smokers showed roughly a 27 percent higher risk of coronary heart disease than never-smokers, and roughly a 45 percent higher risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); the increase in lung and upper aerodigestive tract cancers exceeded double. Smoking a pipe alone is not considered risk-free either. There is no escape on the nicotine front either: all tobacco products deliver nicotine to the central nervous system and carry a risk of dependence. The details of this subject are covered in the entry on pipes and health.
How It Reads Today

Today the text is evaluated not as a guideline but as an example of community writing. In the time since, medical literature has converged on the view that a product switch cannot be considered a solution to a cigarette habit, and that no tobacco product can be considered safe. The piece's lasting value lies in recording a period's community outlook and the assumptions on which that outlook rested.
This entry is for informational purposes and is not medical advice. Decisions about quitting tobacco use should be made in consultation with a physician.

r.x: Pipes and tobacco in the old trade press

covers the pipe-related records accumulated in trade journals, consular and commercial reports, and industrial encyclopedias from the mid-19th century to the first quarter of the 20th. This body of material is considered the main artery of pipe historiography; it speaks in the language of the workshop, the timber yard, and the customs ledger. The same pages also carry the earliest known written trace of several origin legends still in circulation today. American pipe writer Ben Rapaport's selection of excerpts, published on Pipedia and gathered from scattered periodicals, displays this dual character with its collected examples.
Pages That Speak in Numbers

These publications are most solid where they describe the countable. A tobacco history from 1901 records that roughly forty tons of raw briar arrived in London annually, and that Nuremberg and Ruhla each turned out half a million pipes a year. A forestry journal from the same year notes that the blocks were cut to about twenty-five sizes across three basic shapes ("Marseillaise," "Relevé," and "Belgian"). A 1921 US Department of Commerce report states that roughly six thousand tons of root were extracted annually in Corsica, and that of the 1,813 tons of raw block that left the island in 1911, 1,505 tons went to Saint-Claude. A 1936 woodworking manual reports that blocks, boiled and dried for months and then rested for up to two years, were cut into seventy distinct sizes, yielding between seven hundred and nine hundred models. Each of these figures rests on a single period publication; none has been independently tested.
Details from the Workshop

This same solidity continues in descriptions of visible processes. In 1912, a tobacco workers' journal listed apple, pear, peach, plum, hazel, maple, and oak among the woods used for briar fakes on the market. A 1907 journal writes that smokers preferred an amber mouthpiece, an ebonite (vulcanite) one as second choice, and avoided celluloid. According to a 1918 article on the Saint-Claude workshops, flaws in the bowl were filled with a paste that hardened on drying and withstood heat, the surface was corrected with sandpaper and pumice, and the pipe was then dipped in different baths depending on its grade: ordinary pieces got a dark bath to hide flaws, while a fine-grained block got a colorless oil bath that brought out the wood's lines. This shows that the debate over fills has a century-old history. An 1851 industrial encyclopedia likewise records that meerschaum pipes were dipped in melted tallow, then in white wax, and polished with horsetail plant.
Where the Origin Stories Crack

The weakness begins the moment these same publications reach the question of "who was first." The story of the Hungarian cobbler Karl Kovacs, cited as the man who carved the first meerschaum pipe, is repeated in period pages almost as fact; yet no document confirms this name — all that exists is the material's first recorded use as a pipe, dated to around 1723. The name itself has produced a separate misconception: because it means "sea foam" in German, the stone was believed to be gathered from the sea, when in fact it is mined. The origin of the calabash pipe, meanwhile, is attributed to a British soldier who fitted the mouthpiece of his broken pipe into a gourd found in the field; the story entered an 1912 pharmacy journal with the caveat "as it is told," and the chain of sourcing stops there.
Dates That Don't Hold Up

To see how shaky the dates can be, it is enough to set two records side by side. A 1965 geography journal writes that the first briar pipe was made in 1879 by a French craftsman who came to England; yet an 1864 agricultural journal already describes a "briar-root" pipe with a silver band and a goose-bone shank. A similar looseness appears in company histories. An Irish industry book published in 1920 states that Charles Peterson began making briar and meerschaum pipes in Dublin "about forty-five years ago." Company records, however, trace the founding to 1865 and to the Kapp brothers, who came from Nuremberg; according to the records, Peterson joined the business later as a third partner, and the moisture-chamber mechanism bearing his name was patented in 1894. The ten-year gap between the roughly-1875 pointed to by the book and the 1865 given by the company shows how the "approximately" of period texts turned into a precise date in later retellings. The pattern that emerges is clear: this press is reliable when describing material, process, and trade volume, and weak when it comes to claims of priority and founding. Any sentence containing the words "first," "invented," or "discovered" should be read with caution unless backed by an independent document.

r.x: Yenice tobacco

is an Oriental leaf named after the town known in Ottoman times as Karasu Yenicesi. In Western languages it is written "Yenidje" or "Yenidze." The town survives today in Greece's Xanthi region under the name Genisea. The name's transfer to the leaf has more to do with where it was marketed than where it was grown: leaf gathered from surrounding villages changed hands at the Yenice market before being shipped to Europe.
Geography and Character

Yenice is not a botanical variety in its own right but a leaf type produced by a particular basin. In commercial classification it falls under the Basma branch of the Oriental tobacco family; the Xanthi leaf is generally regarded as a grade of Basma. Basma is a small-leaved, fine-textured group low in nicotine; after picking it is strung and sun-cured. In trade classification the Yenice name is tied to the small, fine-veined, oily leaves coming from the Yaka and Cebel branches of Xanthi. The nature of the soil, summer heat, and the leaf's small size are among the factors cited as giving Oriental leaves their characteristic aroma.

What built Yenice's reputation was that it added a sweet, resinous layer alongside the herbal, spicy note common to the family. Blenders' descriptions also attribute a creamy softness to the leaf; these descriptions rest on tasting language rather than a measurable standard. The epithet "queen of tobaccos," used in tobacco trade circles for the leaf, is also passed down as an old phrase; where it was first said is unknown.
Its Place in Industry

From the late 19th century to the mid-20th, the Yenice name was used as a mark of quality. In London in 1913, a company called Yenidje Tobacco Company Limited was founded through a partnership between Louis Rothman and Markus Weinberg; after a falling-out between the two partners the company was wound up by court order in 1916, and today it is remembered more for a landmark case in English company law than for tobacco. In Germany, the tobacco and cigarette factory Hugo Zietz founded in Dresden took the name Yenidze directly; built between 1907 and 1909, the building — notable for its dome and minaret-like chimneys — served as an architectural advertisement announcing the origin of the leaf it processed, and today it is used as office space.

On the pipe side, the name is most associated with Balkan Sobranie: the emphasis placed on Yenice leaf on the label of the blend's white tins is considered a key part of the reputation built around the concept of the Balkan blend. The same leaf was also sought after for the Oriental component of Latakia-forward English blends.
Status Today

The aura around the Yenice name is partly fed by conflicting sources. It is said that the town that hosted the leaf's historic market was badly damaged by a flood disaster in the mid-19th century; though this story is repeated within the community, it has not been anchored to a documented record. Tobacco farming has nevertheless continued in the basin that gave the name its origin. Today the leaf grown in the region is not held as a separate Yenice class in commercial purchasing, so it is not a material accessible to blenders. Products on the market carrying this name are mostly regarded as interpretations following the trail of the old recipe.

r.x: Pipe tobacco

is tobacco prepared for smoking in a pipe, and it differs from cigarette tobacco in two respects: it is noticeably more coarsely cut and kept noticeably moister. Neither of these two properties is arbitrary. Leaf cut too finely packs tightly in the bowl and restricts airflow; leaf that has lost its moisture burns quickly and is spent before it can release its flavor. Nearly all commercial products are made not from a single leaf variety but from a combination of several varieties in set proportions; this combination is called a blend.
The Leaves That Make Up a Blend

Behind hundreds of blends stand a limited handful of core leaf varieties. Virginia is processed by flue-curing, has a high natural sugar content, and forms the backbone of most blends. Burley is air-cured; low in sugar, slow-burning. This makes it well suited both as a base leaf and as a flavor carrier. In the US, roughly seventy percent of Burley production takes place in Kentucky and twenty percent in Tennessee; outside the country, Brazil, Malawi, and Argentina are cited as the main producers.

Latakia is a leaf taking its name from the Syrian port city of Latakia. It is first sun-dried, then left in aromatic wood smoke; Cyprus production uses species such as mastic, myrtle, and Aleppo pine. The resulting smoky character is considered too dominant to be smoked on its own, so Latakia appears in a blend only in accent quantities. Production has over time shifted its weight from Syria to Cyprus. Oriental tobaccos, native to the eastern Mediterranean, meanwhile bring dried-herb and spice notes to a blend.

Cavendish stands apart from this list because it is not a variety but a method: leaf is pressed into a cake, fermented under fire or steam heat, then sliced. It is most commonly applied to Virginia and Burley. Its name is generally accepted to come from the 16th-century English mariner Sir Thomas Cavendish.
Processing and Flavoring

Flavoring is done in two separate stages, and the two are frequently confused. Casing is applied before the cut, in the form of a sugar- and flavor-carrying solution soaked into the leaf; because it sits within the leaf's structure, it retains its presence throughout the smoke. Top dressing, on the other hand, is sprayed onto the surface after the blend has been assembled; being made of volatile compounds, it largely disappears once the tobacco is left exposed to air. Most tobaccos on the market are considered to be cased to some degree.

The most common classification of blends also stems from this distinction. Those carrying a pronounced flavoring are called aromatic; those whose taste comes purely from the leaf composition are called non-aromatic. The line is not always sharp; many lightly cased products fall between the two definitions.
Cut and Storage

Cut styles fall into two logics: the leaf is either chopped directly, or first compressed and then sliced. The most common of the chopped forms is ribbon, arriving as strips roughly one and a half to two and a half millimeters wide; the very finest of these is called shag. In pressed tobaccos, the leaf is turned into a block under heat, steam, and pressure: the block itself is called plug, and the thin slices taken from it are called flake. Rope, twisted like a cord, is likewise used by being cut into thin discs. Cut determines not just appearance; it also dictates how much preparation the tobacco needs before being packed into a pipe and how fast it will burn.

Whatever the cut, pipe tobacco dries when it comes into contact with air, and leaf that has lost its moisture also gives up a significant portion of its flavor. This is why storage takes place in tightly sealed jars or sealed containers.

r.x: Cavendish

, despite what its name suggests, is not a tobacco variety but a processing and cutting method. Dried tobacco leaf — most often Virginia or Burley — is softened with steam and heat, pressed into cakes under heavy pressure, and left to ferment. The resulting dark, soft, sweet tobacco is considered the fundamental building block especially of aromatic blends.
The Process and the Origin of the Name

In typical Cavendish production, the tobacco is first steamed, opening the leaf's pores. The leaves are then pressed into cakes and put through fermentation, heated by fire or steam. Once fermentation is complete, the cakes are sliced and are ready to be blended. This process caramelizes the leaf's natural sugar; the tobacco's harshness softens and its sweetness becomes pronounced.

The name is said to derive from the 16th-century English seafarer Sir Thomas Cavendish. According to the account, Cavendish, on his 1585 voyage to Virginia, moistened tobacco leaves with sugar and bound them tightly, and the tobacco stored this way was found to taste noticeably better. This story, however, is poorly documented and is quite plausibly an origin legend attached after the fact. What is certain is that the name is now used the world over to describe this processing method.
Main Types
Cavendish is not a single recipe but a family of methods. Three main approaches are distinguished:
English-style Cavendish:

Considered the additive-free approach. Only heavy Virginia leaf is held under high pressure for three or four days; the sweetness comes entirely from the caramelization of the leaf's own sugar. This method is known to have been shaped by England's older purity laws restricting additives to tobacco; the generalization that "English Cavendish is always additive-free," however, is not an absolute rule for today's producers.
Danish-Dutch-style Cavendish:

After the tobacco is steamed and its pores opened, it is heavily cased with sugar, fruit, vanilla, and similar ingredients and pressed in a mold. This method forms the basis of modern aromatics; the details of casing and topping are described in the entry on casing and flavoring.
Black Cavendish:
Tobacco darkened thoroughly through additional steaming and "sweating." It is generally produced on a Burley base in the United States and on a Virginia base in Europe.
Common flavors used in Cavendish tobaccos include vanilla, cherry, maple, honey, chocolate, rum, coconut, and whiskey.
Its Place in the Blend

Cavendish adds fullness, sweetness, and softness to a blend; it burns slowly and its room note is generally found pleasant. These qualities make it a staple component both in aromatic blends and in mild mixtures aimed at newcomers.

The quality difference is largely sought in the quality of the base leaf and the degree of casing: over-cased Cavendish burns wet and can lead to the burning sensation known as tongue bite. Another distinguishing point is its relationship with aging. Because Cavendish is already a fermented tobacco, it is considered to be affected comparatively little by aging, while the added flavors fade over time; for this reason, cased Cavendish blends are considered better suited to smoking fresh than to long-term cellaring.

r.x: Dunhill Cigars

is the heading covering the cigar arm of the London firm Alfred Dunhill, known for pipes and pipe tobacco. The firm's relationship with the Havana cigar reaches back to the start of the twentieth century, but a cigar directly bearing the "Dunhill" name only reached shelves in the mid-1980s, and it passed into history within a decade. Today the brand name in tobacco products belongs to a different group entirely.
The Early Tie to Havana

The tobacconist's shop Alfred Dunhill opened on Duke Street in London in 1907 quickly became known for its own blends and its white-dot pipes. On the cigar side, the firm's role for a long time was to be selective rather than to be a producer: before the Cuban Revolution it had distribution agreements with many Havana factories, and sizes available only at Dunhill counters were sold under the name "Selección Suprema." Brand histories also repeat, as a detail cementing the shop's reputation, that George VI and Winston Churchill were among its customers.
Three Exclusive Brands After the Revolution

After 1959 the counterparty changed but the tie did not break; agreements were now conducted with the state monopoly, Cubatabaco. According to the records, exclusive rights to three brands were granted to Dunhill, each tied to a separate Havana factory. Don Cándido, made at the Briones Montoto factory (formerly Romeo y Julieta), was the name with the oldest origin; the brand had been founded in 1935 by Cándido Vega Díaz. Don Alfredo, the product of the José Martí factory (formerly H. Upmann), was born in the 1960s and took its name from the firm's founder. The history of La Flor del Punto, made at the Partagás factory, is the least certain; it is thought to have appeared in the 1970s. The word "punto" means "dot" in Spanish, and Dunhill's exclusive cigar bands also used a white-dot emblem; whether this overlap was deliberate is not certain.
The Cuban Cigar Bearing the Dunhill Name

The cigar bearing the Dunhill name went on sale in 1984: first in Dunhill stores in ten countries, then in nearly thirty. There were eight handmade sizes: alongside the robusto-length Cabinetta and the churchill-length Estupendos, the range included a presidente over twenty-three centimeters long called Havana Club, a long panetela named Atado, a lonsdale called Malecon, a corona called Mojito, and Tubo and Veradero. A few more names appeared in the catalog but were never actually produced. The agreement had been signed in 1982; according to the records, negotiations had begun back in 1977.

What cut the series' life short was competition. Cubatabaco was producing the other top-tier private label of the period, Davidoff, at the same time, and had no intention of taking sides in the market rivalry between the two tobacconists. Sources disagree on exactly which year the agreement ended: some records give 1989, others 1991. What is consistent is that the agreement was not renewed.
After Cuba, and the Brand Changing Hands

Before the split became final, Dunhill had already considered the Canary Islands, the Dominican Republic, and Honduras for production; in the years that followed, lines blended with non-Cuban leaf were produced in the latter two countries. The firm eventually withdrew from the cigar business altogether and transferred the right to use its name on tobacco products.

This transfer is part of a larger split in the company's structure. The majority of Alfred Dunhill's shares passed to Carreras Tobacco Company in 1967; in the years that followed, the tobacco and luxury-goods arms went their separate ways. Today the pipe and luxury-goods side belongs to Richemont, while tobacco products — including the tobacco blends — belong to British American Tobacco, which acquired Rothmans International in 1999. The same name belonging to different owners across different products is a lasting source of confusion for collectors trying to trace the brand's history; a similar case is seen with the tins licensed for production in Germany.
